title: Why children and most students shouldn't be held responsible when they negatively affect their own learning.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton argues, against his own early teaching habits, that children and most students should not be blamed for lacking qualities such as curiosity and resilience that support learning. He separates natural development, such as brain reconfiguration in the early teens and prefrontal maturation later, from learning shaped by repeated experiences, and uses Erikson's stages to show that dispositions are largely formed by what happens to children. Children arrive at school with genes, womb experiences and early care they did not choose, so these qualities are things to be taught rather than assumed. He compares them with maths: nobody blames a child for not yet multiplying, and the same logic should apply to personal qualities. He accepts that suspension is sometimes necessary, and concedes legal responsibility at around sixteen, but insists schools avoid compounding matters through shame.
points: Responsibility for poor learning dispositions cannot sensibly be pinned on children until after middle schooling, since they have little control over genes, early care or developmental timing.
Distinguishing natural development from learning shows which parts of a child are out of anyone's control and which can be taught.
Erikson's stages suggest that many dispositions are causally shaped by early experience, so they behave more like learned than innate traits.
Including personal qualities among a school's intended outcomes implies treating them like academic subjects, moving from beginning to developing to mastering.
Blaming students is comforting for teachers but wrong, and even suspension should be treated as a learning event that avoids deepening shame.
quotes: Now, after a long time spent around learning, I no longer believe in holding young children and most students responsible for the positive or negative contribution they make to their own learning, even on a broad scale. Ot, at least, I can’t even think of holding them responsible until their middle schooling, up to and around fourteen, has been fully completed.

They simply aren’t there yet. There’s much learning still to do. I could no more hold them responsible for not yet being resilient as I could hold a first-time skier responsible for not yet being able to navigate more difficult black runs.

It’s why teaching is so important to learning. On a daily basis children and students receive either accidental or deliberate helpful or unhelpful repeated experiences, from their teachers and others, that help them hardwire so much that is good or not so good.
When learning isn’t happening, there’s something comforting about blaming the child or the student. But it’s wrong.

It makes the assumption that schools don’t expect these qualities to exist already; it accepts that, with their support and that of others, children and students will get better at their personal development in the same way that they get better at being able to do math or any other subject. They will move from beginning, to developing to mastering, over time.

That’s exactly what we should do for children who don’t yet have the qualities that would help them become better learners. We shouldn’t blame them. We should take on the commitment to help them get better.
But the suspension itself also causes learning to happen of some kind. We need to make sure it is a process that doesn’t compound matters by creating shame and more.
